subjects.name: Water Supply Systems
defs: The water pipe that connects one fixture to a distribution branch or directly to a water main.
A private water source serving one or more families that is not an approved public water supply.
A piped water system serving the public that has at least 15 service connections or serves 25 people daily for at least 60 days a year.
A vertical water supply pipe that extends one story or more to feed branches or a group of fixtures.
Piping inside a building or on the premises that carries water from the service pipe or meter to the points of use.
A public water supply pipe, or system of pipes, installed and maintained by a public entity in a street or public easement.
The pipe that carries potable water from the water main, or from the meter at the right of way, to the building distribution system.
The water service pipe, distribution piping, fittings, control valves, and appurtenances that deliver potable water within or adjacent to a building.
The length of a pipeline measured along the centerline of the pipe and its fittings.
The smallest cross-sectional area at a water discharge point, expressed as the diameter of an equivalent circle.
The pressure in a water supply pipe at a fixture outlet while that outlet is fully open and flowing.
Backpressure of 4.33 psi or less, equal to the pressure exerted by a column of water 10 feet high.
A valve installed where static pressure exceeds 80 psi to reduce building water pressure to 80 psi or less.
Any pressure lower than the pressure exerted by the atmosphere at the same location.
A pump, hydropneumatic tank, or elevated tank that supplements pressure when the available supply cannot meet fixture demand.
A device that absorbs the pressure surge created when water flow in a supply system stops suddenly.
Chlorinated polyvinyl chloride pipe listed for water service and hot water distribution rated at 100 psi and 180 degrees Fahrenheit.
Copper tube made in Types K, L, and M and listed for water service and distribution piping.
Cross-linked polyethylene tubing listed for water service and for both hot and cold water distribution.
A cement-mortar-lined iron pipe listed for water service and water distribution mains.
Zinc-coated steel pipe listed for water service and distribution and joined by threads or mechanical fittings.
Solder and flux containing not more than 0.2 percent lead, required for joints in potable water supply piping.
A pipe of cross-linked polyethylene layers bonded to an aluminum core, listed for water service and distribution.
Polyethylene tubing formulated for raised-temperature service and listed for hot and cold water distribution.
The maximum pressure a pipe or tube is rated to withstand in service, at least 160 psi at 73.4 degrees Fahrenheit for buried service pipe.
A connecting device that joins pipes or fittings of different sizes or types that do not otherwise fit together.
A valve on a pressurized supply line that opens to deliver a measured flush and closes gradually to reseal the fixture trap.
A shutoff valve whose fully open closure member does not restrict flow through the valve body.
A valve with a wedge-shaped gate that lifts fully out of the flow path when the stem turns.
A pipe connection that relies on compression or an elastomeric seal rather than solder, solvent cement, threads, or heat fusion.
A permanent mechanical joint with an elastomeric seal, made with a pressing tool and jaw approved by the fitting manufacturer.
A mechanical fitting that seals by inserting the pipe or tube into the fitting body.
A valve or faucet that shuts off rapidly, either automatically on release or through a mechanical fast-closing mechanism.
A fitting that taps a branch into an existing pipe, prohibited as a joint in water supply piping.
A hot water distribution system with pumps that circulate heated water from the heater through supply piping and back.
A recirculation system that starts its pump only when a user signals demand, then primes the hot water piping.
Water at a temperature of 110 degrees Fahrenheit or higher, the code threshold for hot water supply.
A combination valve that opens on excess temperature or excess pressure to protect a water heater tank.
Water held between 85 and 110 degrees Fahrenheit for bathing and washing where full hot water would scald.
A device on the cold water inlet that absorbs the volume increase created as water is heated in a closed system.
A valve that admits air to prevent a vacuum from forming inside a water heater or storage tank.
An appliance that heats potable water and delivers it to the potable hot water distribution system.

subjects.name: Drain-Waste-Vent
defs: Any part of a plumbing piping system other than a riser, main, or stack.
Lowest portion of a building's drainage piping that receives soil and waste discharge and carries it to the building sewer.
Pipe that begins at the end of the building drain and carries its discharge to a public sewer or private disposal system.
Piping within a public or private premises that conveys sewage, rainwater, or other liquid waste to a point of disposal.
Drain pipe that connects one or more fixture drains to a soil stack, waste stack, or building drain.
Liquid waste that reaches the drainage system through a receptor or air break instead of a direct pipe connection.
Piping that carries sewage and other liquid waste from fixtures to a public sewer or private disposal system.
Receptacle and pump assembly that lifts sewage from a point below the gravity drain to a higher line.
Drain pipe that carries sewage containing fecal matter to a building drain or building sewer.
Vertical line of soil, waste, or vent piping that extends through at least one story, with or without offsets.
Piping and receptors that collect rainwater and surface water and carry it to a point of disposal.
Pipe that carries only liquid waste that contains no fecal matter.
Steady drainage discharge, such as from a pump, rated at two fixture units per gallon per minute.
Unit that expresses the probable drainage load a fixture places on the drainage system.
Total drainage fixture units connected to a pipe segment, used to select its required diameter.
Drainage load from equipment that discharges in bursts and is rated in fixture units by flow rate.
Arrangement of bends that shifts one section of pipe out of line with but parallel to another section.
Total fixture units that discharge into a vertical stack, checked against the maximum its diameter permits.
Receptor installed outdoors to collect surface water and direct it into a storm drainage line.
Device that closes a drainage line automatically to stop sewage from reversing into a building.
Access opening in a drainage line that permits removal of a blockage with a plug, cap, or removable fixture.
Assembly of a wye and a bend that produces a smooth, sweeping change of direction between drain pipes.
Fitting intended for drainage service, with a recessed, smooth interior waterway that leaves no ridge inside the pipe.
Fitting that changes drainage flow direction by 45 degrees.
Fixture or surfaced area that receives liquid waste and discharges it through a trap.
Tee fitting with a curved inlet that turns flow from a horizontal branch into a vertical stack in the direction of drainage.
Fitting with a long, gradual curve that carries flow through a change of direction with little resistance.
Y-shaped fitting that joins a branch to a drain at a shallow angle so flow turns gradually.
Vent that connects one or more individual vents to a vent stack or stack vent.
Waste piping arrangement that vents fixtures through an oversized common pipe instead of separate vent piping.
Vent that connects a soil or waste stack to a vent stack to equalize pressure between them.
Reverse pitch that makes a drain fall away from its point of disposal and hold water.
Vertical drop of a pipe over a stated horizontal distance.
Rate at which a horizontal drain falls toward the point of disposal, commonly stated in inches per foot.
Sudden rise in water depth where flow slows at a change from steep to flat grade.
Interior bottom surface of a pipe at a cross section, used as the reference for elevation.
Slope expressed as vertical drop divided by horizontal run, then multiplied by one hundred.
Flow speed that keeps solids suspended and clears settled sediment from a sloping drain.
Fall of a pipe stated as vertical drop per unit of horizontal run.
Pitch of a trap arm, commonly one-quarter inch per foot, that keeps the arm self-scouring.
Continuous, unbroken pitch along a drain run, without flat or reversed sections.
Pitch of a vent pipe that lets moisture drain back by gravity to the pipe it serves.

subjects.name: Traps and Vents
defs: Installing two traps in series on one fixture drain is prohibited.
The drain pipe that carries waste from a fixture trap to the next drain junction.
A trap shaped so flowing waste clears solids from its interior without relying on partitions.
The short pipe that carries waste from a fixture outlet down to the trap inlet.
A fitting or device that holds a liquid seal to keep sewer gas out while wastewater passes.
The section of fixture drain that runs from the trap outlet to the vent connection.
The highest point of the internal passage at the lowest part of the trap bend.
The low point at the outlet side of a trap over which the seal spills.
Pressure in the drainage piping that pushes against the trap seal from the outlet side.
A cover or membrane that slows evaporation from the seal of a floor drain trap.
The drawing of liquid into a narrow space by surface tension, which can pull water out of a trap seal.
The amount of liquid that must leave a full trap before air can pass.
The slow loss of a trap seal as water turns to vapor during long disuse.
The vertical distance from the trap weir down to the top of the trap dip.
A device that adds a measured amount of water to a trap that is seldom used.
The loss of a trap seal when negative pressure in the drain pulls the water out.
A one-way valve that admits air when negative pressure develops and seals when flow stops.
A branch vent that serves two to eight traps connected to one horizontal branch.
A vent that connects at the junction of two fixture drains and serves both traps.
A vent pipe that serves one fixture trap and connects to the vent system at a higher level.
A vent for a sink or lavatory that rises past the fixture outlet before dropping below the floor.
A vent that circulates air between drainage and vent systems or relieves stack pressure.
Piping that supplies air to a drainage system and protects trap seals from pressure changes.
Outdoor end of a vent pipe that opens to the atmosphere for air exchange.
A vent that also carries wastewater from fixtures on the same drainage branch.
A stack height of at least eight feet within which one floor's branches connect.
The smallest allowed vent diameter, one and one-quarter inches, before sizing tables require more.
The extension of a soil or waste stack upward past the highest horizontal drain connected to it.
A vent that terminates separately to open air from a sewage ejector or sump.
The maximum drainage load a vent of a given size can serve under the adopted code tables.
A common vent pipe that joins several stack vents at the top and runs outdoors.
A vertical vent pipe that provides air circulation to and from the drainage system.
A bell-shaped trap below a floor drain inlet that collects debris and is prohibited.
A trap in a building drain that prevents air movement between the building and sewer.
A vent connected at the trap crown too near the weir to protect the seal.
A cylindrical trap with a vertical axis, prohibited except for solids or chemical waste.
A vent run that is level or back-pitched, so it traps water and blocks air.
Ice can block a vent terminal in cold weather unless the terminal is increased in diameter.
A trap whose outlet turns downward right after the seal, forming an S that siphons.
A trap with no protecting vent, leaving its seal exposed to siphonage and backpressure.

subjects.name: Backflow and Fixtures
defs: The flow of water or other substances into potable distribution pipes from a source other than the intended one.
Pressure in a connected system that exceeds supply pressure and drives water toward the potable main.
Backflow caused by negative pressure in the potable water distribution piping.
An impairment of potable water quality that creates a public health hazard through poisoning or disease.
Any physical connection between a potable water system and a source of contamination or pollution.
Water unsuitable for drinking, bathing, or culinary purposes because of its quality.
An impairment of potable water quality that harms appearance, taste, or odor without creating a health hazard.
Water safe for drinking, bathing, and culinary use because harmful impurities fall below hazardous levels.
The unobstructed vertical distance through free atmosphere between a water outlet and the flood level rim below it.
A device that admits air downstream when supply pressure drops and protects only against backsiphonage.
A device, assembly, or method that stops backflow from entering the potable water supply.
A continuous pipe loop rising about 35 feet that prevents backsiphonage but not backpressure.
The minimum height above a flood level rim at which a backflow preventer or vacuum breaker must sit.
A testable assembly of two check valves used to protect against low or moderate hazards.
A non-testable pair of check valves installed on a residential service, immediately downstream of the meter.
A vacuum breaker threaded onto a hose bibb that stops backsiphonage from a hose or attached appliance.
A testable vacuum breaker with a spring-loaded check and shutoff valves that may operate under constant pressure.
A testable assembly with two check valves and a relief valve that vents the zone between them to atmosphere.
A vacuum breaker assembly with a check valve and air-inlet vent that limits water spilled from the vent port.
A bathing fixture with a waste outlet of at least 1 1/2 inches and, where fitted, an overflow of the same size.
A fixture connected to potable water and drainage that delivers a stream of water for drinking.
A drain inlet with a removable strainer and an outlet of at least 2 inches in diameter.
A hand-washing basin fixture that requires a waste outlet at least 1 1/4 inches in diameter.
A receptacle or device connected to a water supply, a drainage system, or both.
A bathing area with a shower head, a compartment of at least 900 square inches, and a waste outlet of at least 1 1/2 inches.
A basin fixture whose waste outlet must be at least 1 1/2 inches in diameter and fitted with a strainer.
A fixture that receives liquid waste and flushes it through a trap into the drainage system.
A toilet fixture that receives liquid and solid waste and removes it by flushing into the drainage system.
A plumbing fixture installed to meet the reach and clearance rules of ICC A117.1.
A piping arrangement in which a drain discharges below a flood level rim and above a trap seal.
The 15-inch minimum distance from a fixture centerline to a side wall, partition, or obstruction.
The edge of a receptacle over which water overflows when the fixture is filled.
The count of plumbing fixtures an occupancy requires, set by use and occupant load in Table 403.1.
Toilet rooms provided for each sex wherever plumbing fixtures are required.
A divider between urinals that provides privacy and leaves at least 30 inches between partitions.
An enclosure with walls or partitions and a door that separates a public or employee water closet.
A flushing feature that provides a reduced volume for liquid waste and a full volume for solid waste.
The quantity of water a water closet or urinal uses in one flushing cycle.
The highest water use the code allows for a fixture or fitting, listed in Table 604.4.
Nonpotable water produced by treating wastewater at a permitted facility for approved uses.
An EPA labeling program for fixtures and fittings that are independently certified for water efficiency and performance.
A tank-type toilet certified to use no more than 1.28 gallons per flush and meet performance criteria.

subjects.name: Plumbing Code
defs: A plumbing system that satisfies the code's intent and performance level even though the code does not specifically regulate its design.
Acceptable to the code official, who may require tests or research reports as evidence of compliance.
An established and recognized organization regularly engaged in testing, inspection, or product certification that the code official has accepted.
The officer or other designated authority charged with administering and enforcing the code, including a duly authorized representative.
A plumbing system legally installed before the code took effect or covered by a permit to install that has already been issued.
A legally adopted set of minimum requirements governing the design, installation, and maintenance of plumbing systems.
The water distribution pipes, fixtures, traps, soil and vent pipes, drains, and appurtenances within a structure, including the water service and building sewer.
A product whose function and performance an approved agency has tested and continues to monitor under a certification program.
A permit letting a qualified tradesperson make repeated alterations to an approved system without obtaining a separate permit each time.
An appointed body that hears appeals of the code official's orders, decisions, and code interpretations.
Written, graphic, and pictorial material describing a project's design, location, and physical characteristics for permit review.
An inspection made when the building is complete, fixtures are connected, and the structure is ready for occupancy.
A written notice the code official issues after tests and inspections show the work complies with the code.
Official authorization the code official issues before regulated plumbing work may begin.
An inspection made after framing and all sanitary, storm, and water piping are installed but before wall or ceiling membranes.
A written order halting work that is proceeding contrary to the code or in a dangerous manner.
An inspection made after trenches are excavated and bedded and piping installed, but before backfill is placed.
A copper joint made by heating cleaned surfaces and melting a filler metal that conforms to the applicable filler standard.
A fitting that joins copper or copper-alloy tubing to steel pipe while preventing galvanic corrosion between the different metals.
A connection the code forbids, such as a cement joint, saddle fitting, or solvent-cement joint between different plastics.
A copper joint made by cleaning surfaces, applying flux, and melting lead-free solder to draw into the gap.
A plastic pipe adhesive that softens and fuses the mating surfaces of pipe and fitting as it cures.
A plastic pipe joint made by coating clean surfaces with solvent cement and assembling them while the cement remains wet.
A screwed connection in which tapered external pipe threads engage internal threads and seal with compound or tape.
A pipe connection formed by heating two ends until they fuse, with or without added filler metal.
The prepared trench bottom or placed material that gives continuous load-bearing support along a buried pipe.
The depth below grade to which soil freezes, used to set minimum burial depth for exterior water piping.
The maximum distance allowed between supports for a given piping material, size, and orientation.
A larger pipe built into a foundation wall so the passing pipe can move without loading the wall.
A steel plate protecting pipe installed close to the edge of a bored or notched framing member.
Devices that support and secure pipe, fixtures, and equipment in a plumbing system.
Rigid bracing installed where flow direction changes in large horizontal drains to resist movement from flow forces.
A test that pressurizes nonplastic piping with air and holds the pressure to reveal leaks.
A worker able to identify existing and predictable hazards and authorized to take prompt corrective action.
A space large enough to enter, with restricted entry or exit, that is not designed for continuous occupancy.
An atmosphere that may cause death, incapacitation, injury, or acute illness through fire or explosion, oxygen imbalance, or toxicity.
A confined space containing a hazardous atmosphere, engulfment potential, converging walls, or another serious safety hazard.
A method such as sloping, benching, shoring, or shielding that protects workers from cave-ins and falling material.
A test that fills traps with water and introduces pungent smoke to find openings in the drainage system.
A test that fills drainage piping with water to a specified head and holds it to reveal leaks.
